Pool Tile Cleaning in Phoenix, AZ

That white crust along the waterline is not dirt. It is minerals left behind as Valley water evaporates. One free call, any hour, puts you through to an independent, locally owned pool service company that can look at it.

  2. Services
  3. Pool Tile Cleaning

Pool tile cleaning in Phoenix, AZ is mostly about one thing: the white or gray line that creeps along the tile at the water's edge. In the Valley it can come back faster than pool owners in milder places expect. The reason is not a lazy pool cleaner. It is the combination of hard tap water and a lot of evaporation.

This page explains how that line forms, the two kinds of scale and why they matter, the methods pool companies use to remove them and what each can damage, and how to slow the line down once the tile is clean. It also answers two questions people often ask: whether muriatic acid or a melamine sponge is safe to use.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro does not clean tile. It is a free phone line. Call (623) 240-0428 any hour, an automated assistant asks what you are seeing, and you are put through to an independent, locally owned pool service company. That company looks at the tile, quotes, does the work and bills you directly.

Why calcium lines form so fast in Phoenix pools

When pool water evaporates, the water leaves but the dissolved minerals stay. Every time the pool is topped off with fresh tap water, more minerals go in. Over months, the water holds more calcium than it can keep dissolved, and the extra starts to settle out as scale. The waterline is where it shows first, because the tile there is wet and then dry, again and again, as the level rises and falls.

Phoenix speeds up every part of that cycle. The Arizona Department of Water Resources says the average evaporation rate in Phoenix is about six feet of water a year, most of it in summer. A table published by the City of Scottsdale for a 400 square foot pool shows evaporation peaking at about 10.8 inches in June and dropping to about 2.6 inches in January. That is a lot of water to replace, and the replacement water is hard: the City of Phoenix's 2025 water quality report lists total hardness of 172 to 302 parts per million in its system. The city explains that this hardness comes from calcium and magnesium the source water picks up from soil on its way to the treatment plants.

Heat plays a part too. Calcium carbonate is less soluble in warm water, so a pool industry water balance note points out that scale tends to show first in the warmest spots, such as a sunny tile line or a spa.

Two kinds of tile scale: the kind acid dissolves and the kind it does not

Not every white crust at the waterline is the same mineral. Most is calcium carbonate, but some deposits shrug off acid, which changes how they have to come off. It is worth asking which kind the company sees.

Comparison of calcium carbonate scale and acid resistant scale on pool tile
What to compareCalcium carbonateAcid resistant deposits
How it reacts to acidDissolves in acid at room temperature, so a professional descaler can soften itRoom temperature acid does little; one industry case turned out to be calcium sulfate, confirmed by lab testing
How it usually comes offLight buildup can respond to gentle hand work or a pool professional's descalerUsually needs mechanical removal, such as bead blasting or pumice, by a professional
What to askCan this come off by hand without blasting?Which method will you use, and what will it do to my tile and grout?

A careful pool technician tests a small area before choosing a method, because the right approach depends on both the scale and the tile.

How pool companies remove tile scale, and what can go wrong

There are three main approaches. Each one works on some scale and can damage some surfaces, so the right choice depends on what your tile is made of and how stubborn the buildup is.

Media blasting

A machine blows a fine media, often glass beads, against the tile. Trade articles describe it as a gentler cousin of sandblasting and a common choice for stubborn scale along a whole waterline. The water is usually lowered below the tile line first.

Risks: not every tile suits blasting, so a small test spot comes first. The wrong media or too much force can damage glaze or grout, and spent media lands in the pool and on the deck and has to be cleaned up.

Hand work

A pumice stone, tile brush or plastic scraper used by hand on wet tile. It suits small areas, light buildup and touch ups between bigger cleanings.

Risks: a trade article on tile scale warns that pumice is aggressive enough to take a little of the glaze off along with the scale, so it is not for every tile. Metal tools and wire brushes scratch tile too.

Chemical descalers

Acid based gel cleaners and other descalers applied by a professional to soften scale, often together with hand work. They can help on calcium carbonate, not on deposits that resist acid. The water is lowered below the tile so the acid stays off the plaster.

Risks: acids can etch grout, plaster and some glazes, give off fumes and throw off the pool's water balance. This is professional work, not a homeowner project.

What to expect on a tile cleaning visit

A typical job starts with a look at the tile, the grout and the type of scale, and a test on a small spot. If the method calls for it, the water level is lowered below the tile line. The City of Phoenix says pool water must not go to the storm drain; it belongs in the sanitary sewer cleanout or on plants. Ask where any water that is pumped out will go, and check your own city's rule if you live outside Phoenix. After the cleaning, the pool is refilled to its normal level and the water is tested, because fresh fill water and any cleaning products change the balance.

Cleaning sometimes uncovers loose, cracked or missing tiles and crumbling grout that the scale was hiding. Those are repairs, not cleaning. A cracked tile line can also be a sign of movement or a leak, which is covered on our pool leak and crack repair page and the general pool repair page.

Muriatic acid and melamine sponges: the safe answers

Muriatic acid on pool tile

Muriatic acid is a form of hydrochloric acid. It is corrosive, it releases fumes that hurt eyes and lungs, and it can etch grout, plaster and some tile finishes. It also lowers the pool's pH and alkalinity if it drips in. This page does not give acid instructions, on purpose. Leave acid work to a pool professional.

Never mix pool chemicals with each other, and never combine acid with chlorine products, which can release toxic gas. Store pool chemicals apart, dry, shaded and out of children's reach, and follow every label.

Melamine sponges on pool tile

A melamine foam sponge is a very mild abrasive once wet. Many owners use it on smooth tile at the waterline for light film and spotting. It will not remove hard mineral scale, and like any abrasive it may leave a haze on glossy or glass tile.

Test a small spot you do not usually see first. Use it only on light film, rinse the area and stop if the finish looks different.

How often to clean pool tile, and how to slow the scale down

Light film should come off as part of regular cleaning, whether you do it or a weekly service does. A deeper descaling is needed when the band is visible and brushing no longer moves it. How often that happens varies from pool to pool. The real answer is to stop the scale forming in the first place.

Keep the water balanced

Scale forms when the water is more saturated with calcium carbonate than it can hold. Pool professionals measure this with the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI), a single number built from pH, alkalinity, calcium hardness, water temperature and total dissolved solids. A reading near zero means the water is balanced. A positive reading means the water tends to leave scale behind; a negative reading means it tends to eat at plaster and grout. Because water temperature is part of the formula, water that is balanced in March can turn scale forming in July. A good weekly service tests for this and adjusts with the seasons. Our pool cleaning and weekly maintenance page covers what that service includes.

  • Test the water regularly with a home test kit and keep pH from drifting high.
  • Brush the waterline when you brush the pool, before film hardens.
  • Watch the water level. Keep it steady at the middle of the skimmer opening so the same strip of tile is not wetting and drying all day.
  • Use a cover when the pool is not in use. The Arizona Department of Water Resources says pool covers can cut evaporation by 90 to 95 percent, and less evaporation means less top off water and fewer added minerals.
  • Ask about high mineral water. When calcium and dissolved solids climb too high, the long term fix is replacing some or all of the water. The City of Phoenix says draining should be infrequent; our guide to how often to drain a pool in Arizona explains the choices.

Questions to ask before tile cleaning starts

  • Is this ordinary calcium scale, or a kind that acid will not dissolve?
  • Which method and which media will you use, and have you tested it on a small spot?
  • How much water will be lowered, and where will it go?
  • What happens if loose tile or failing grout turns up?
  • Will you test and rebalance the water afterward?
  • Is the price written, and does it include cleanup of media from the pool and deck?
  • If any repair is included, what is your ROC license number?

Common questions

Can you use muriatic acid to clean pool tile?

Muriatic acid is a strong hydrochloric acid, and pool professionals do use acids on some scale. It is not a homeowner job. It gives off harsh fumes, burns skin and eyes, can etch grout, plaster and some tile glazes, and it changes the pool's chemistry when it drips into the water. Never mix it with chlorine or any other pool chemical. Leave acid work to a pool professional who can protect the surfaces and rebalance the water afterward.

Can you use a magic eraser on pool tile?

A melamine foam sponge acts as a very mild abrasive when wet. Many pool owners use one on smooth waterline tile to lift light film and early spotting. It is not much help against hard mineral scale, and because it is still an abrasive, some owners warn it can leave a haze on glass or glossy tile. Try it gently on a small, hidden spot first, and stop if the finish changes.

How often should pool tile be cleaned in Phoenix?

There is no set calendar. Brushing the waterline during regular cleaning keeps light film from building up, and a deeper scale removal is done when a white or gray band is visible and will not brush off. How fast that happens depends on your water balance, how much water evaporates and gets topped off, and whether the pool is covered.

How much does pool tile cleaning cost?

The line does not set or quote prices. The pool company you reach prices the job after seeing it. What drives the price is the length of the tile line, how thick and how hard the scale is, which method it needs, whether the water level has to be lowered, and whether any grout or tiles need repair. Get the price in writing before anyone starts. Our pool service cost guide explains other pool costs in Phoenix.

When cleaning pool tile, what should you avoid?

Avoid metal scrapers, wire brushes and coarse scouring pads, which scratch glaze. Avoid household cleaners and acids in the pool, and never combine cleaning products or pool chemicals. Avoid scrubbing glass tile with pumice. Use a soft pool brush or a tile brush for routine cleaning, and call a pool company for scale that will not come off with gentle brushing.
